description: Sixteen candidate reforms; current-law baselines and examples must be verified against original sources. This is not a judgment that any law or person is corrupt.

pillars.name: Close the side doors
pillars.question: Can public offices enforce fair rules?

records.title: Faster political-money disclosure
records.short: See major funding before Election Day.
records.baseline: Federal committees generally disclose on reporting schedules; certain independent expenditures already trigger 24- or 48-hour reports.
records.proposal: Require machine-readable reporting within 24–48 hours during election periods for contributions above a proposed $200 threshold and qualifying expenditures.
records.benefit: Voters can investigate late-cycle funding before casting ballots.
records.tradeoff: Faster filing raises compliance costs and may require exemptions or safeguards for low-risk small organizations.
records.measure: Median hours between transaction and public release; share of filings arriving before Election Day.

records.title: Reveal hidden funding vehicles
records.short: Identify organizational funders when the law permits.
records.baseline: Most 501(c)(4) organizations do not publicly disclose contributor names on IRS Schedule B; organizational payments alone cannot establish original donor identity.
records.proposal: Require enhanced beneficial-owner and source-of-funds reporting for qualifying election communications above a proposed $10,000 organizational spending threshold.
records.benefit: Reduce opportunities to conceal election-related financial flows behind opaque entities.
records.tradeoff: Privacy, associational freedom, safety, and constitutional challenges; disclosure must be carefully tailored.
records.measure: Share of qualifying spending with publicly validated source attribution, versus unknown origin.

records.title: Political-ad transparency
records.short: Know who bought, targeted, and paid for an ad.
records.baseline: Existing advertising disclosures vary by ad type, platform, and jurisdiction; one comprehensive public archive is not assumed.
records.proposal: Establish standardized records for ad purchaser, spend, dates, geographic targeting, and available aggregate audience information.
records.benefit: Expose fragmented ad purchases and inconsistent messages across audiences.
records.tradeoff: Protect user privacy, prevent disclosure of sensitive audience identities, and avoid publishing unsafe microtargeting details.
records.measure: Percent of qualifying ads with searchable purchaser, spend, and targeting metadata.

records.title: Account for in-kind access
records.short: Track trips, retreats, services, and noncash support.
records.baseline: In-kind campaign support, gifts, travel, and lobbying have different legal reporting regimes; they cannot be combined without classification.
records.proposal: Harmonize cross-references for reportable travel, retreats, logistical support, policy services, and other benefits.
records.benefit: Make noncash benefits easier to examine alongside political spending.
records.tradeoff: Legitimate meetings, legal advice, policy discussion, and non-reportable personal activity need clear boundaries.
records.measure: Share of reportable in-kind benefits with source, recipient, date, and appropriate legal classification.

records.title: Stronger coordination safeguards
records.short: Check when an outside spender is truly independent.
records.baseline: Federal coordination rules already test payment, content, and conduct; shared vendors alone do not prove coordination.
records.proposal: Revisit rules for common consultants, family relationships, staffing, reused campaign materials, and candidate-controlled activities.
records.benefit: Clarify when purportedly independent spending should count as campaign support.
records.tradeoff: Requires precise standards so protected independent political speech is not mislabeled or chilled.
records.measure: Enforcement determinations and substantiated coordination cases—not shared-vendor matches alone.

records.title: Contractor and lobbyist guardrails
records.short: Reduce preferential access tied to donations.
records.baseline: Federal contractor and foreign-national contribution prohibitions already exist; broad lobbyist or foreign-ownership bans are not assumed.
records.proposal: Evaluate expanded restrictions on covered contractors, lobbying-related bundling, and clearly defined influence-conflict situations.
records.benefit: Reduce risks that public procurement or official decisions are perceived as donor-dependent.
records.tradeoff: Overbroad restrictions can conflict with associational rights or treat lawful participation as misconduct.
records.measure: Political contributions or bundled funds from legally covered entities before and after policy changes.

records.title: Separate lawmaking and fundraising
records.short: Protect official time from campaign fundraising.
records.baseline: Restrictions already govern some fundraising on federal premises; comprehensive legislative-session-hour bans are additional proposals.
records.proposal: Restrict covered officeholders from soliciting political funds during official legislative session hours, with enforceable definitions.
records.benefit: Reduce visible overlap between public duties and campaign fundraising.
records.tradeoff: Time-zone, remote-work, enforcement, and speech concerns require narrow drafting.
records.measure: Verified fundraising events or solicitations overlapping prohibited official periods.

records.title: Explore constitutional spending limits
records.short: What would it take to cap independent spending?
records.baseline: Supreme Court precedents including Buckley and Citizens United constrain broad limits on independent political expenditures.
records.proposal: Assess an amendment authorizing legislatures to establish constitutionally permissible election-spending limits.
records.benefit: Could alter the constitutional authority available for limits on independent spending.
records.tradeoff: Amendment ratification is difficult and would prompt major debate over speech and association rights.
records.measure: Legal milestones, ratification status, and subsequent spending concentration; not speculative savings.

records.title: Match small donations with public funds
records.short: Make a $25 donation worth more to a qualifying campaign.
records.baseline: New York City already operates an optional small-donor program with an 8:1 match for qualified contributions, subject to limits and eligibility rules.
records.proposal: Evaluate 6:1 or 8:1 public matches for the first $200 from qualifying local donors, paired with spending and contribution rules.
records.benefit: Increase campaign incentives to seek many modest contributions.
records.tradeoff: Public funding cost, candidate eligibility, fairness across districts, and oversight must be assessed.
records.measure: Number of unique in-district contributors, share of receipts from small donors, program cost.

records.title: Democracy vouchers
records.short: Give eligible residents a campaign-funding voice.
records.route: State/local pilot; federal legislation for expansion
records.baseline: Seattle uses publicly funded democracy vouchers; eligibility and voucher amounts vary by election.
records.proposal: Study a model such as four $25 publicly funded vouchers per eligible resident.
records.benefit: Can enable participation by residents who cannot spare cash for donations.
records.tradeoff: Administrative expense, take-up inequality, program funding, and fraud controls matter.
records.measure: Voucher redemption by geography and participation group, candidate breadth, program cost.

records.title: Independent district maps
records.short: Make district boundaries less dependent on lawmakers.
records.baseline: State redistricting institutions differ; some jurisdictions already have independent or bipartisan commissions.
records.proposal: Expand independently administered, transparent mapmaking with published evaluation criteria.
records.benefit: Can reduce direct legislative control over district boundaries.
records.tradeoff: Commission selection, litigation, community representation, and measurable fairness are complex.
records.measure: Competition, representational bias, map transparency, and compliance with voting-rights law.

records.title: Compare alternative voting systems
records.short: Test whether different ballots change competition.
records.route: State/local election law; federal legislation for federal rules
records.baseline: Ranked-choice and other voting methods are used in selected jurisdictions, but election rules vary and impacts are context-dependent.
records.proposal: Study ranked-choice or approval voting for eligible elections with pilots and independent evaluations.
records.benefit: May change candidate incentives and voter choice depending on design.
records.tradeoff: Education, ballot complexity, implementation costs, and uncertain partisan effects.
records.measure: Exhausted ballots, voter understanding, participation, competitiveness, and representation.

records.title: Reform federal enforcement
records.baseline: The FEC is legally structured for six commissioners and needs four affirmative votes for official action.
records.proposal: Evaluate an odd-numbered commission, independent leadership, stronger procedural tools, and faster penalties.
records.benefit: Potentially reduce deadlock and case backlogs.
records.tradeoff: Agency independence, appointment politics, due process, and investigative-power checks need careful design.
records.measure: Case age, substantiated enforcement rate, vacancies, and enforcement backlog.

records.title: Limit officials' individual-stock trading
records.short: Reduce financial conflicts in public office.
records.baseline: Financial disclosure and STOCK Act rules exist; a universal individual-stock ban for all covered officials and families is a separate proposal.
records.proposal: Examine limits on covered individual securities trading and supervised diversified or trust alternatives.
records.benefit: Could reduce avoidable conflicts and increase public trust.
records.tradeoff: Family coverage, asset definitions, divestment taxes, enforcement, and blind-trust design are consequential.
records.measure: Reportable trades, late disclosures, documented conflicts, and enforcement outcomes.

records.title: Longer revolving-door safeguards
records.short: Limit rapid monetization of government relationships.
records.baseline: Existing post-employment restrictions vary by role and conduct; they are not a uniform five-year paid-advisory ban.
records.proposal: Explore a five-year cooling-off period for specified lobbying and paid advisory activity with tightly drafted coverage.
records.benefit: Could reduce incentives to favor future private employers.
records.tradeoff: Employment restrictions, constitutional concerns, enforceability, and compensation effects.
records.measure: Covered employment transitions, violations, waivers, and procurement/regulatory conflict patterns.

records.title: Protect people who report violations
records.short: Make it safer to document wrongdoing.
records.baseline: Whistleblower protections vary by agency, occupation, and statute; campaign-vendor protections are not uniformly comprehensive.
records.proposal: Study safe reporting channels, anti-retaliation rules, independent review, and carefully bounded financial awards.
records.benefit: Help investigators verify illicit coordination or unlawful funding with firsthand evidence.
records.tradeoff: False-report safeguards, witness privacy, due process, and incentive design are essential.
records.measure: Verified complaints, retaliation findings, processing time, and substantiated recoveries.
